analysis.one_liner: Phases out the government's direct student loan program and returns all lending to banks.
analysis.headline: Backed by 30 Republican cosponsors, the bill never left subcommittee and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997, leaving the federal direct student loan program in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have phased out the Federal Direct Student Loan Program — the government-run lending program created in 1993 — by capping it at 5% of new loans in 1995-96 and allowing none after that, then repealing its legal authority outright. It would have auctioned off the government's entire direct loan portfolio to private buyers and moved all federal student lending back into the bank-based guaranteed loan program, where private lenders receive federal subsidies and the government covers most defaults. It also rewrote federal budget rules so that administrative costs counted against direct lending but not against bank-based loans.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, guaranty agencies, and student loan secondary markets such as Sallie Mae would have gained the entire federal student loan market, since the bill eliminates the government's competing direct lending program and routes every borrower back through the guaranteed program, where lenders earn federal subsidies and are shielded from most default losses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan banks and guaranty agencies

how_it_helps.text: Caps direct federal student loans at 5% of new loan volume for the 1995-96 academic year and prohibits any direct loans after that, repealing the program's legal authority as of October 1, 1997 — permanently removing the government-run alternative to bank-based lending.

Requires the Education Department to auction off its entire portfolio of direct loans to private buyers, with the first sale within 120 days and the loans sold free of federal guarantees or further federal regulation, converting public assets into purchases for private financial firms.

Rewrites the federal credit-reform accounting rules to charge administrative and oversight expenses only against large direct loan programs — those making $5 billion or more in commitments a year, which in practice means direct lending — making direct loans score as costlier in the budget while leaving the subsidized guaranteed loan program out of that accounting.

Bars the Education Department from spending any funds on public relations or marketing to encourage schools to participate in direct lending, and forbids further upgrades to the program's software, hobbling the program during its phase-out.

analysis.who_pays: Students and families would lose the direct loan option and be routed entirely through bank-based loans, and taxpayers would continue paying the subsidies and default guarantees that keep private lenders in the guaranteed program. The Treasury would also absorb whatever shortfall arises if the auctioned loan portfolios sell for less than their value, since the first sales would carry no federal guarantee.

drawbacks.text: Every borrower would be forced into the bank-based guaranteed loan channel, where the government pays lenders subsidies and guarantees them against most defaults — so any savings from shutting down the federal bureaucracy would come at the price of larger payments to private lenders.

The new accounting rules apply only to loan programs with $5 billion or more in annual commitments — in practice, direct lending — while the guaranteed loan program is exempt from the same treatment, so the bill tilts the budget comparison toward its preferred outcome rather than measuring both programs the same way.

The bill itself requires the Education Secretary to report whether the auction results 'represent a true reflection' of the true subsidy cost of the loans — an acknowledgment that selling the portfolios without federal guarantees, starting within 120 days, might fetch less than the loans are worth, with the proceeds going to the Treasury.

Schools and borrowers who had just switched to direct lending would face a second major disruption: the bill requires modifying or phasing out agreements with institutions within two academic years, with no transition protection built in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's case rested on its claim that private lending is more efficient and that direct lending would add roughly 500 federal employees and 15,000 contract workers. But the bill offered borrowers nothing except the loss of the government-run loan option, and its own accounting changes were drawn to apply to direct lending alone, which weakens the claim that the comparison was honest. Whatever administrative savings were real would likely be offset by the subsidies and default guarantees the guaranteed program pays out to banks on every loan. As designed, the bill's benefits flowed to the lending industry and its costs to borrowers and taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to their subcommittees, which never held a markup or vote, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Ernest Istook introduced the Student Loan Privatization Act on April 7, 1995, joined by 20 original cosponsors named on the bill, and 30 Republicans cosponsored in total.
The Speaker referred it to both the Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee and the Government Reform and Oversight Committee on the day it was introduced.

Within three weeks it was sent to the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology (April 25) and the Subcommittee on Postsecondary Education, Training and Life-Long Learning (April 28).
The sponsor delivered introductory remarks on June 9, 1995, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever recorded; the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student borrowers kept the government-run direct loan option, and the guaranteed student loan industry lost its best chance that session to eliminate its public competitor by statute.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student borrowers who kept the direct loan option

for.name: Ernest Istook
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 7, 1995 and delivered introductory remarks on it June 9, 1995.

for.name: 30 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

for.name: Guaranteed student loan industry (banks, guaranty agencies, and Sallie Mae)
for.role: Lenders and secondary market in the bank-based guaranteed loan program
for.what_they_did: Lobbied through this period to protect the guaranteed lending program from the government's direct lending competitor, which the bill would have abolished.

against.name: Subcommittee on Postsecondary Education, Training and Life-Long Learning (House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee)
against.role: Subcommittee with jurisdiction over the Higher Education Act
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 28, 1995 and never reported it out; no markup or vote was ever held.

against.name: Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology (House Government Reform and Oversight Committee)
against.role: Subcommittee with jurisdiction over the budget-accounting provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 25, 1995 and never took further action on it.

against.name: Clinton administration
against.what_they_did: Defended the direct student loan program, its signature 1993 initiative, against Republican efforts to phase it out during 1995.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors and the sponsor were Republicans, with no Democratic support, and although Republicans controlled the House the bill still never reached a committee vote.

industries.industry: Student loan banks, guaranty agencies, and secondary markets (e.g., Sallie Mae)
industries.note: The bill would hand the industry the entire federal student loan market by repealing the government's direct lending program and auctioning its portfolio to private buyers. Lenders profit in the guaranteed program from federal subsidies and default guarantees, so their gain here comes at the expense of the cheaper public alternative that borrowers and taxpayers were using.

Schools would lose the choice to participate in direct lending and would have to rework participation agreements within two academic years, but the bill promises lighter regulation and paperwork under the guaranteed program.
